title: Mattei v. Hopper
summary: A good-faith satisfaction condition limited the purchaser’s discretion and supplied an enforceable obligation.
notes:
Court: Supreme Court of California (1958).

The notes ask how approval by an attorney, time allowed to obtain leases, and a promise’s conditions should be interpreted. Good faith here operates in identifying an existing obligation; the course’s later, broader unit on performance in good faith is not imported.

sections.Parties: Mattei, a real-estate developer, sued Hopper, the landowner, over a contract to buy property for a shopping-center project.
sections.Material Facts: The price was $57,500, with a $1,000 deposit and a 120-day period. The arrangement was subject to Mattei’s obtaining leases satisfactory to him. Hopper declined to proceed and argued that the satisfaction clause left Mattei free to perform or not, making the contract illusory.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court ruled against Mattei on the enforceability issue. The Supreme Court of California reversed. The excerpt resolves the asserted failure of consideration; it does not provide a final damages award.
sections.Issue: Did the purchaser’s satisfaction condition leave the promise so discretionary that no consideration or mutual obligation existed?
sections.Holding: No. The duty to exercise judgment in good faith supplied a real limitation on the purchaser’s discretion.
sections.Reasoning: The opinion distinguishes satisfaction concerning commercial value or operative fitness, often measured by reasonableness, from matters involving personal judgment, assessed through honest dissatisfaction. A package of prospective leases involves many factors, including tenant quality and suitability to the development, that do not reduce to one objective measure. Good faith therefore constrains Mattei. A condition limiting when performance becomes due does not itself establish an absence of contractual commitment.
